title: yamt
tagline: A three-way merge window like the one in JetBrains IDEs, for every git conflict at once. 🔀
why: JetBrains IDE's three-pane merge window is the only merge tool I find usable. VS Code's merge editor, its extensions and the TUI mergetools all felt unintuitive.

They all start from the `<<<<<<<` conflict markers. Once git has collapsed a merge into markers the base is gone, so you can see _that_ two sides differ but not _what each side changed_. yamt never parses a conflict marker: it reads the base, your side and theirs from git's index and diffs them itself.

`git mergetool` opens one file at a time, and real merges touch many files. yamt takes over the whole merge: every conflicted file in one window, your side on the left, theirs on the right, the result in the middle.

sections.title: Install
body: Download from the [releases page](../../releases):
- **Linux**: the `.AppImage` or the `.deb`. The `.deb` (`sudo apt install ./yamt_0.4.0_amd64.deb`)
puts `yamt` on your PATH. For the AppImage, put it there yourself.
Without AppImageLauncher:
```sh
install -Dm755 yamt_0.4.0_amd64.AppImage ~/.local/bin/yamt
With AppImageLauncher (it stops a copy outside its folder with a dialog): let it integrate the
AppImage (it moves the file to `~/Applications` and adds a hash to the name) and link the moved
file:
```sh
ail-cli integrate yamt_0.4.0_amd64.AppImage
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && ln -sf ~/Applications/yamt_0.4.0_amd64_*.AppImage ~/.local/bin/yamt
If `yamt` is then not found, `~/.local/bin` is not on your PATH: add
`export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"` to your shell's start-up file (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`).
- **Arch Linux**: the AppImage, or build from source (below).
- **macOS**: the `.dmg`; drag yamt to Applications. The build is not signed, so macOS refuses to open it
("damaged", or "could not verify … free of malware") until you clear the download mark from the whole app.
Do this after every install or update:
```sh
xattr -cr /Applications/yamt.app
Then put `yamt` on your PATH (once):
```sh
sudo mkdir -p /usr/local/bin && sudo ln -sf /Applications/yamt.app/Contents/MacOS/yamt /usr/local/bin/yamt
- **Windows 10/11**: the `_x64-setup.exe`; it installs for your user only, without admin rights.
The build is not signed, so SmartScreen may warn: More info → Run anyway. yamt needs
[Git for Windows](https://git-scm.com/download/win) (`git.exe` on your PATH). The installer does
not put `yamt` on your PATH: add the folder its setup page installed to (under Windows'
Environment Variables, user `Path`), then open a new terminal. yamt is a console program: run it
from a terminal in the repository; started from the Start menu a console window opens beside it.

sections.title: Use
body: When `git merge`, `git rebase` or `git cherry-pick` stops with conflicts, run `yamt` in the repository (or `yamt --repo <path>` from anywhere). yamt starts from a terminal inside a repository; double-clicking it in a file manager or Finder shows nothing.
bullets: The file list on the left shows every conflicted file with git's view of it (resolved or not, also when you run `git add` elsewhere); click one to open it. Drag its edge to make it wider. The button at the right of its "Files" header shows it as a tree, folders first with VS Code's folder icons, and back as a list (remembered after a restart). Ctrl+B (Cmd+B on macOS) hides and shows the list.

The left pane's header names what is checked out: the branch, or the commit and its subject when no branch is (during a rebase). The right pane's header names what you are merging in: the branch, or the commit and its subject.

Lines that no change touches are collapsed behind a wavy line across all three panes, keeping 4 lines next to each change, so every change of a file is in view with little scrolling. Click the wave (in any pane or between them) to show 4 more lines next to each change, again for 8 more, a third time for the rest. Searching for text in hidden lines shows them. The toolbar's "Collapse unchanged fragments" button turns collapsing off and on again for every open file.

Each change has an arrow that applies it to the result and a × that ignores it; press one and drag up or down to apply or ignore several at once (one undo step). On a conflict, Ctrl+click (Cmd+click on macOS) on the arrow also ignores the other side, and on the × also takes the other side; holding Ctrl (Cmd) when releasing a drag does the same for every conflict it covers. Ctrl+click (Cmd+click) a highlighted change applies it, Ctrl+right-click (Cmd+right-click) ignores it. The toolbar applies all non-conflicting changes from the left or from the right in one click.

From the keyboard: click a side or one of its changes (an outline shows which), then Enter or Space applies the change, Backspace, Delete or x ignores it, Up and Down move between the changes still waiting on that side, and Left and Right switch sides. The toolbar's up and down arrows do the same as Up and Down (on the left side when no side has the keyboard). Ctrl+scroll (Cmd+scroll on macOS) over a side steps through its changes. Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z (Cmd on macOS) undo and redo from anywhere in the window. These are the default keys; settings can change them.

Hold Alt (Option on macOS) for a minimap of the result over the right pane's right edge: its code in syntax colours, language-server errors and warnings on its left edge, the changes still waiting on its right edge, and a box over the part on screen. Click a line to bring it to the middle of the result, or drag the box or scroll over the minimap; the cursor and the keyboard stay where they were. Releasing Alt hides it.
The result pane is a normal editor: type, Tab / Shift+Tab indent and outdent, undo and redo. Ctrl+F (Cmd+F) finds text in whichever pane you clicked.

The gear at the toolbar's right end opens settings: **Dark** or **Light** colours, on Linux **Subpixel** (colour-edged text like WebStorm's, the default) or **Greyscale** antialiasing, every yamt shortcut — add, change or remove a key per action, or reset it (a key another action uses asks before moving) — and the language servers (below). Settings are saved per user in `~/.config/yamt/settings.json` (`~/Library/Application Support/yamt/settings.json` on macOS, `%APPDATA%\yamt\settings.json` on Windows) and hold only what you changed; point the settings page at another file, for example in your dotfiles, and yamt reads and writes that one, picking up your edits whenever its window gets focus.

Ctrl+S (Cmd+S on macOS) saves the result to the file without staging it, so you can stop and come back later: changes still waiting are written as git wrote them (a conflict as its conflict markers), and yamt finds them again next time. A dot at the right end of the Result header shows unsaved work; closing the window asks only when something is not saved.

**Mark resolved** writes the result, stages the file and opens the next unresolved one. It turns blue once nothing is left to process. **Reset**, next to "Result", brings the file back as it was when this run of yamt opened it.

Right-click the toolbar to choose which of its icon buttons show (abort merge, previous/next change, collapse unchanged fragments, apply all from either side, undo, redo; Abort merge, Undo and Redo start hidden). The choice applies to every file and is remembered after a restart; the keys work either way.

A file deleted on one side and changed on the other shows the changed side with its changes, and two buttons: **Keep** and **Delete**. Other files the editor cannot show (binary, symlinks, submodules) get a choice between the two sides.
Closing the window exits with status 0 when every file is resolved and 1 otherwise, so scripts can tell. Then continue as usual (`git commit`, `git rebase --continue`, …).

**Abort merge** (shown from the toolbar's right-click menu, then right after Mark resolved; only during a `git merge`) runs `git merge --abort` after one question, so every resolution and save is lost and the repository goes back to how it was before the merge. yamt then closes with status 1. Untracked files and changes from before the merge in files it did not touch stay; if git refuses (for example a file staged and then changed again), yamt shows git's message and changes nothing.

sections.title: Language servers
body: yamt runs the language servers your project already has, so the result pane shows their problems as you type: an underline, with the message on hover. It finds these in the repository's projects and asks once per repository whether to start them; settings can change the answer:
- JavaScript and TypeScript: oxlint, oxfmt, Biome, TypeScript, eslint; `.vue` files through TypeScript when the project has `@vue/typescript-plugin`
- Rust: rust-analyzer · Go: gopls · C and C++: clangd, with a compile database
- Python: ruff, ty, basedpyright, pyright
- PHP: Phpactor, with the project's own PHPStan, Psalm, PHP-CS-Fixer and phpcs; else Intelephense

Left of the gear, each server shows its state; click one to start, stop or restart it or to read its log. A server the project uses but that is not installed shows "Not installed" with the install command for that language's installer (your package manager, uv, Poetry or PDM, rustup, `go install`); yamt starts it when you come back to the window. With a formatter running (oxfmt, Biome, rustfmt, gofmt, ruff, clang-format with a `.clang-format`, PHP-CS-Fixer or phpcbf, or an added server that formats), Ctrl+S formats the result before saving and leaves changes that still wait as they are. yamt ships no language server.

Other servers are added in settings under **Language servers → Added by you**: pick one **From the list** (Deno and bash-language-server are there too) or type a command and the file types it serves. yamt looks for a program in the project's `node_modules/.bin`, `.venv/bin` and `vendor/bin` up to the repository root, then on the PATH of the terminal it was started from, then in `~/go/bin`, `~/.cargo/bin`, `~/.local/bin` and Composer's global folder; a command with a `/` is read from the repository root. An added server is offered in every repository and runs where the repository's answer is Start; press **Start** under "This repository" if it is not.

sections.title: Make it feel built in
body: ```sh
git config --global alias.resolve '!yamt'
git resolve
`git mergetool` is not the way to start yamt: it runs the tool once per file, while yamt handles all files in one window.

sections.title: Build from source
body: You need the Rust toolchain from `rust-toolchain.toml` (installed by [rustup](https://rustup.rs) on the first `cargo` call), [pnpm](https://pnpm.io), and on Linux webkit2gtk-4.1 (Arch: `webkit2gtk-4.1`; Debian/Ubuntu: `libwebkit2gtk-4.1-dev`).
```sh
cargo install tauri-cli --version 2.12.1
pnpm -C frontend install
cargo tauri build
The bundles land in `target/release/bundle/`.

sections.title: NVIDIA on Linux
sections.body: WebKitGTK's DMABUF renderer crashes on some NVIDIA setups. yamt switches it off by itself when the NVIDIA driver is loaded; a value you set for `WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER` wins.
